chapter_theme: The second part of the Valaik Kummi maps the body as a cosmos in which the Maiden lives: the lamp that burns in the six houses without oil, the breath (வாசி) to be practised through the nostril, Sadasiva at the brow, Maheswara at the throat, Rudra in the heart, Vishnu at the navel and Brahma at the root, the body as a chariot of five hundred nails and a fort of nine gates. The letters of the mantra are placed in the body too (நகார, வகார, உகார, மகார, சிகார), Om is said to hold the mute letter, and the stanzas on the untied bull and the dying body make the point of the map: the deity is in the body and men die without seeing her. The chapter closes in cipher, riddles of flower, fruit and sons, and a place-name map from Melur to Kaalur.
structure_note: 1889 to 1894 follow the lamp of 1888 into the breath practice and the upper house; 1895 to 1899 place the five gods in the body from brow to root; 1900 to 1902 figure the body as chariot and fort and ask why men die with the deity inside; 1903 to 1905 place the letters and Om; 1906 and 1907 are on taming the breath before the body dies; 1908 to 1911 are riddles of conception; 1912 and 1913 read the body as a map of towns and a burning fort.

1889.reading: It burns in the house of six, and there is no oil in it and no nectar-water; the way to go is seen, yet there is no path; the path is tangled, tangled, Maiden.
1889.nuance: ஆறு வீடு is read as the six adharas, the centres of the yogic body, in which the Maiden's lamp of 1888 burns without fuel, which is the point: her light is not fed. பாதை சிக்குது, the tangled path, is the central channel the breath must find. அமிழ்தண்ணீர் may be the nectar of the head or plain water for a lamp.

1890.reading: It is heard like the ring of anklets; the tangled path is very steep; the right-whorled conch sounds; above, look at the breath, Maiden.
1890.nuance: Anklet-sound and conch are the inner sounds (நாதம்) heard as the breath rises; tradition lists them among the ten sounds of yoga. துடுக்கம் (steepness, or roughness) is the difficulty of the channel. The stanza joins sound and breath without explaining how one leads to the other.

1891.reading: One must know the practice of the breath, and build the houses of the mandala; taking the way of the nostril, see the aim of yoga and of the breath, Maiden.
1891.nuance: நாசி வழி, the nostril's way, is the plainest statement in the song that the practice is breath control. மண்டல வீடுகள் கட்ட (building the mandala-houses) is unclear: the centres as houses to be built up, or the period of a mandala (forty-eight days) of practice.

1892.reading: Within the three-flamed lamp, in the practice of the breath in the root mandala, whatever flame it becomes, that flame is the Maiden; there is none other than her, Maiden.
1892.nuance: முச்சுடர் is the three lights, sun, moon and fire, taken in yoga as the three channels or the three eyes; the Maiden is the flame they become in the root centre. The stanza identifies goddess, flame and breath-result in one line.

1893.reading: Because the Maiden stays unheated and is within the Siva perfected by the horse, let us look at the practice of the breath without leaving it; we can see the upper house, Maiden.
1893.nuance: The stanza is cipher: சூடாமல் (without heating, or without crowning) may mean the kundalini not yet roused; பரி சித்த சிவன் is the Siva accomplished through the horse, the breath. மேல்வீடு, the upper house, is the head centre and also release; both senses stand.

1894.reading: He who saw the upper house is the skilled one; he who stood in the lamp in the sky is the one of speech; he who saw the mother's house is the knower; he who leapt the horse is the soldier.
1894.nuance: Four names are given for four attainments; பாணி, வாணி and பட்டாணி may be puns on hand, speech and the Pathan soldier, rhymed with ஞானி. The one who leaps the horse (பரி தாண்டிக் கொண்டான்) is the one who has passed beyond the breath. The sense of each title is tradition's guess.

1895.reading: The hand in the fig, the mind in devotion, in the intellect in the very middle; the forehead is Sadasiva, I have said; look at your own state, Maiden.
1895.nuance: The first line is a rhyming cipher (அத்தி, பத்தி, புத்தி, மத்தி) whose terms are unclear; அத்தி may be fig, elephant or bone (அஸ்தி). The one clear claim begins the body-map: Sadasiva, the highest of the five, at the forehead.

1896.reading: In the press I told the five letters; I praised them in the fruit of knowledge; at the throat there is Maheswara too; see with the eye and look, Maiden.
1896.nuance: The map continues: Maheswara at the throat, below Sadasiva at the brow. அழுத்தில் and பழத்தில் are rhymes for கழுத்தில் and are read as the pressing (of the breath) and the fruit (of knowledge); they may be filler.

1897.reading: In the five, in the tender one, you creeper-women who daily play fondly: in the heart Rudra stays all round; he is straight with you, Maiden.
1897.nuance: Rudra at the heart is the third station of the map. அஞ்சிலே பிஞ்சிலே is cipher, perhaps the five (elements or senses) and the young fruit (the embryo) of 1908; the address to the dancing women is the kummi's frame.

1898.reading: In the belly, in the middle row, in firm thought, before you: in the navel Vishnu too stays; see this truly, Maiden.
1898.nuance: Vishnu at the navel, the fourth station. உந்தி is the navel and, in older Tamil, the breath's base; the stanza asks that the placement be seen as true (உண்மையாய்), not taken on faith.

1899.reading: In the banyan, in this world, in the time to come, in what is favourable: at the root Brahma stays, finishing the breath and holding the body, Maiden.
1899.nuance: Brahma at the root completes the five gods from brow to base, which is the Saiva order of the five faces turned into a body-map. வாசி முடிக்கிறான் பிண்டம் பிடிக்கிறான் makes Brahma the one who ends the breath and seizes the body, a creator who is also the maker of death; the first line is rhyming filler.

1900.reading: There is a chariot with five hundred nails; in it there are gods and there is music; see who is there: the Maiden deity is contained in it, Maiden.
1900.nuance: The chariot is the body; ஐஞ்சூறு ஆணி (five hundred nails) is probably a count of bones or joints, though tradition gives several numbers. The gods and music are the five of the preceding stanzas and the inner sounds of 1890.

1901.reading: There is a fort with nine gates; inside it the keepers of the post are five; with love, the attendants are six; it is contained there, Maiden.
1901.nuance: The nine gates are the body's openings, a stock figure; the five keepers are the senses or the elements, and the six attendants (பரிகாரர்) the six adharas or the six faculties, as tradition takes them. The stanza's point is that the fort is guarded from within.

1902.reading: While the deity stays in the body in this way, through what the intellect does not know, men die without seeing the joyful Maiden; what is this, Maiden?
1902.nuance: The map's conclusion is a complaint: the goddess is in the body and men die anyway. புத்திக்கு அறிக்கையினால் is read as 'because of the intellect's knowing', that is, its wrong knowing; the word is strained.

1903.reading: Because the letter NA became the fixed one, the house became the letter VA of the sky, with grace; the letter U became the head at the crown; look at this closely, Maiden.
1903.nuance: The letters of the mantra are now placed in the body, as Tirumular places them (NA at the feet, MA at the navel). திட்டிப்பு is unclear (fixing, or dizziness); வான வகாரம் makes VA the sky-element, and உகாரம், the U of Om, the crown. The exact placements are the stanza's cipher.

1904.reading: The letter VA became sound; that letter MA became maya; the letter SI became maya too; make this clear and see, Maiden.
1904.nuance: Two letters are given the same value, மாய்கை, which is probably a copyist's repetition; the third line should give SI a different term, perhaps சிவம். Tirumular gives MA to impurity and VA to form (975), so the correspondences are not fixed across the tradition.

1905.reading: There is the syllable Om, and within it there is the mute letter too; now that we have known this letter, seek out the deed and see, Maiden.
1905.nuance: The mute letter is placed inside Om, the half-letter or the silence after the sound, as tradition takes it. வினை நாடிப் பாரடி, seek the deed, is unexpected: knowing the letter is to be tested on karma, or the deed is the practice to be sought.

1906.reading: The untied bull must be tied; desire must be cut; the breath must be joined; the branch out of reach must be bent; how long will the body last, Maiden?
1906.nuance: The bull is the mind, or the breath itself, in tradition's reading; the branch out of reach is the crown the breath must be bent to. The last line gives the reason for haste: the body does not wait.

1907.reading: Staying in the way one was, the breath must be held in without taking more; wandering, running, roaming and burning, the body has died, Maiden.
1907.nuance: வாசி ஏற்காமலே அடக்க (to restrain the breath without receiving it) is read as holding the breath rather than drawing it in; the stanza contrasts the still body with the one worn out by motion. The first line, இருந்த மார்க்கமாய்த் தானிருந்து, is read as staying in one's own state.

1908.reading: From the flower that bloomed there is the young fruit, and there are many young fruits without a flower; by the eldest son there is life, and by the other three there is ruin.
1908.nuance: Cipher. The plain reading is of conception: flower as the woman's period and fruit as the embryo, with fruits without flowers as conceptions that defy the rule. Tradition takes the eldest son as the seed kept (or the breath, or Om) which gives life, and the other three as the three malas or the other three states that waste it. The stanza has no refrain.

1909.reading: Long live the line of chaste women; long live those who gave the chastity they stand by; praising the supreme consciousness, dance the kummi; praising the supreme self, dance the kummi.
1909.nuance: A kummi commonplace, blessing the dancers' chastity, is joined to the praise of சிற்பரன் and தற்பரன், the Supreme as consciousness and as self. கற்பை அளித்தவர் (those who gave chastity) is read as the women's husbands or parents, or the goddess herself.

1910.reading: In the five, two did not perish; in the six, four were not removed; it sleeps in the young fruit and in the flower; it can be tended and set, Maiden.
1910.nuance: Number cipher continuing 1908: five and six may be the elements and the adharas, or the counts of the letters; what sleeps in fruit and flower is the seed or the breath. The arithmetic is not recoverable from the stanza, and the reading keeps to its surface.

1911.reading: The handless dwarf embraced; the legless tall one butted; he dropped it like honey without a bee, and it is no longer sweet, Maiden.
1911.nuance: A riddle in the Siddhars' cipher. The plain reading is of the sexual act and the spending of seed, which the song then calls tasteless; a coded reading takes the dwarf and the tall one as the breath and the mind, and the honey without a bee as the nectar that comes without effort. The stanza fits both and favours neither.

1912.reading: In support of the fort of Melur, the lamp shines well on the Kannanur road; because the hall of Kaalur was left, it is a hard walk, Maiden.
1912.nuance: The towns are body-parts punned into place names: Melur the upper town (the head), Kannanur the eye, Kaalur the foot. Leaving the hall of the feet for the lamp of the head is the ascent of the breath, called a hard walk. The puns are the stanza's whole method.

1913.reading: In the triangular fort within the throat, on the flag-mast fixed and planted there, she fought and came and ran away; the fort burned and became embers, Maiden.
1913.nuance: The triangle at the throat is the vishuddhi centre of the yogic map; the she who fights and flees is the Maiden, or the life, leaving the body, which then burns on the pyre. The stanza is the song's picture of death, the counterpart of the fort of 1901.

links.note: Thirumular Njanam names the root adhara as the circle of three lights and the triangle with three channels, and tells the reader to know the letter A there; Konganar puts the three-flamed lamp in the root mandala and says its flame is the Maiden. Both place the three lights at the root, one ending in a letter and the other in the goddess.

Tirumular puts fire, water, air, sun, moon, Vishnu, Brahma and Rudra all within the heart; Konganar's stanzas 1895 to 1899 distribute the five gods along the body, Sadasiva at the brow, Maheswara at the throat, Rudra in the heart, Vishnu at the navel and Brahma at the root. Only Rudra keeps the same seat; the Siddhar spreads over the body what the Tirumanthiram gathers into one place.

Sangili Siddhar tells the woman that the eight-span body with its nine gates has eight places that appear to those who know its coolness; Konganar's fort of nine gates holds five keepers and six attendants. Both read the body's nine openings as a dwelling with inner stations to be known rather than as the leaking pot of the older ascetic verse.

Tirumular says the Lord set the nine gates as sluices and the fire at the end within the lotus at the head; Konganar's body is a fort of nine gates with keepers within. The nine gates are shared; Tirumular's are channels for what passes, Konganar's are guarded doors.

Tirumular places NA at the feet, MA at the navel, SI and VA at the shoulders and YA as the light above; Konganar places NA as the fixed one, VA as the sky and U at the crown. Both lay the mantra's letters over the body, but neither the letters nor the places agree, which shows the method was shared while the map was not.

Tirumular says that when the silent letter meets the spoken letter the five draw in like a tortoise and Om gains an inner light; Konganar says the mute letter is within Om and that knowing it is the task. Both make the unsounded letter the inside of the sounded syllable.

Tirumular says those who can tie in its stall the frisking calf that butts at the sack will find how the fruit ripens; Konganar says the untied bull must be tied, desire cut and the breath joined before the body fails. The beast to be tied is the mind in both, though Konganar's reading can also make it the breath.

source_issues: 1904: lines 2 and 3 both end மாய்கையாச்சே; one is probably a copyist's repetition and the value given to SI is lost.
1908, 1909 and 1911 to 1913 vary the refrain or lack it; 1909 is a blessing formula of the kummi genre rather than a stanza of the argument.
